Mutagenicity in the Ames test arises through several distinct mechanisms. Context: The Ames test is a bacterial reverse mutation assay that detects compounds capable of inducing genetic damage. Histidine-dependent Salmonella typhimurium (and sometimes E. coli tryptophan auxotrophs) are exposed to the test compound; mutagenic compounds cause reversion mutations that restore the bacteria's ability to synthesize the required amino acid, producing visible colonies. The test is run both with and without metabolic activation (rat liver S9 fraction) to detect pro-mutagens that require CYP-mediated bioactivation.

Mutagenicity in the Ames test arises through several distinct mechanisms. Direct-acting mutagens are electrophilic species that react covalently with DNA bases — alkylating agents (epoxides, aziridines, nitrogen mustards, alkyl halides), Michael acceptors (α,β-unsaturated carbonyls, acrylates, vinyl sulfones), and acylating agents.
